title: ORPHEUS: A Case You and Your Agent Can't Crack Alone
pitch: A detective game where your agent reads every byte of the evidence and sees none of it. 25 WebMCP tools, no screenshot tool, and a case that only closes when the human and the agent both look.
about_excerpt: A detective game where your agent reads every byte of the evidence and sees none of it. 25 WebMCP tools, no screenshot tool, and a case that only closes when the human and the agent both look. Like 1 Comment Story Updates Thumbnail Verification Panel Inspiration Co-op games need a second person. That is why I never play them. Every agent demo I have seen has done the same thing: the agent screenshots the page, clicks the button, and the human watches. The human is a spectator to their own software. I wanted the reverse. An agent that is genuinely powerful and genuinely incomplete, where I am the half it cannot replace. So I asked myself a question: what if the agent could read everything on the page, and see nothing? What it does Orpheus is a co-op detective game you play alone, because your agent is player two. A physicist is dead. His workstation was seized intact. Files, mail, messages, photos, a browser, a terminal, a system log. Every application on that desk is also a tool your agent can call. Twenty-five of them. Your agent can search every file, read every email, and filter fifty-one log entries down to the six that matter. What it cannot do is see. I gave it no screenshot tool, no vision tool, and no pixel access anywhere in the registry. It gets the filename, the camera, the timestamps, and not one pixel. So when the case turns on what is visible in a photograph, it opens the image on your screen and asks you what is in it. You describe. It searches what you described. The case will not unlock until a correlation has run through a tool and you have done your own looking. How I built it I built it using Next.js and React, fully client side. No backend, no database and no sign-up. I set one rule and it carried the whole build: if the human can do it and the agent can do it, the logic exists once. My register.ts declares 25 tools and implements none of them. Each delegates to the same service functions the UI calls, so the agent can never reach state a human could not. I added a static check that fails the build if the tool layer ever imports a data module directly. On top of that, 4 declarative HTML forms using the WebMCP declarative API. Then I added some guardrails: a 1500 character output budget, untrustedContentHint on every tool returning prose the agent did not author, and a nine verb terminal allowlist that refuses rm , chaining, and injection. Challenges I ran into The agent solved the whole case in one turn. It made forty tool calls, then handed me a finished report. I have to say it was correct, but completely against the point. Asking a model to slow down is like asking it not to delete a file. It might comply. It might delete the file anyway. So I put it in the tool layer: after five reads with no human action, read tools stop answering and tell the agent to hand back. I left actuation ungated, because putting a document on my screen is the behaviour I want. My hints made a blind agent sound sighted. They described photo contents to help the player along, so the agent just told the player everything right away. I rewrote every hint to give a location and a question. "The window glass, lower half. Tell me what is there." A tool result silently ate my rules. The output budget trims by halving the longest array, which was the protocol array in the briefing. A model asking for the rules of play was getting one rule of seven, with no sign the rest existed. I found it by measuring the payload instead of trusting it. Accomplishments that I'm proud of The blindness is a mechanic, not a disclaimer. A prompt asking a model not to look is only advice, and it will look anyway if it decides it needs to. Withholding the capability from the registry is a rule. The page audits itself. If you want to test it yourself, open the LINK console and press QUICK VERIFY. 15 checks run against the tool registry in front of you, in your own browser. And it generalises, which I proved instead of claiming. I built a second instance at /apollo13 running the same 25 tools over the real Apollo 13 accident record: the Review Board report, the Mission Report, five voice loop threads, nine NASA photographs with real byte sizes and SHA-256 prefixes you can check yourself. I invented nothing. Where the primary sources contradict each other, I left the contradictions in. A corpus that resolves its own conflicts cannot teach you to find one. Same engine, same tool layer, one data file and a route. All of it is public domain. What I learned Withholding a capability is a design tool, and an underused one. The interesting question is not what else I can let an agent do. It is what it should have to ask me for. And a prompt is not a mechanic. Anything I wanted to actually be true had to live in the tool layer. What's next for ORPHEUS: A Case You and Your Agent Can't Crack Alone My corpus is a single interface, so any archive fits: a leaked document dump, a codebase post-mortem, a medical file, a legal discovery set. The version I want to build next is not fiction. It is the archive where letting an agent click freely is exactly what you cannot allow, and where the person reviewing it needs a partner that can hold fifty thousand files and no judgment at all. live_observation.first_impression: The page loaded with the ORPHEUS title but exposed no interactive elements in the accessibility snapshot. Rendered text was largely inaccessible Next.js payload rather than a usable detective interface.
live_observation.action_attempted: Tried to identify and use the central investigation workflow, but no controls were exposed.
live_observation.after_state: No meaningful UI state change was possible; the page remained non-interactive from the tester's view.
live_observation.notes: The metadata claims a co-op mystery, but the live page did not present an actionable workflow.
